Symptom Guide: Cough
A plain-language reference for community health awareness use
Symptom Overview
Cough is one of the most common symptoms that brings people to a health worker or clinic. It is the body's natural way of clearing the throat and airways of dust, mucus, smoke, or germs. Most coughs are mild and go away on their own within one to two weeks. However, a cough can sometimes be a sign of an infection or other health problem that needs attention, especially if it lasts a long time or comes with other symptoms.
This guide describes cough in general terms. It does not tell you what disease you have. It only explains common reasons a cough may happen, simple steps you can take at home, and signs that mean you should see a health worker or doctor without delay.
Possible Common Causes
A cough can happen for many reasons. Some common ones include:
Common cold or seasonal flu (viral infection of the nose and throat)
Dust, smoke, indoor cooking fumes, or other irritants in the air
Seasonal allergies (reaction to pollen, dust mites, or similar triggers)
Throat irritation from dry air or talking/shouting for long periods
Chest infections such as bronchitis or pneumonia
Ongoing lung conditions such as asthma or chronic bronchitis
Acid reflux (stomach acid rising into the throat)
A cough that lasts two weeks or longer can, in some cases, be linked to tuberculosis (TB), which is an important public health concern in India
This list is only meant to show that many different things can cause a cough. It is not a way to diagnose yourself or anyone else. Only a qualified health worker can determine the actual cause after examination and, if needed, tests.
Self-Care Advice
For a mild, recent cough without warning signs, the following steps may bring comfort while your body recovers:
Drink plenty of clean, safe (boiled or filtered) water and warm fluids
Rest well and avoid overexertion
Gargle with warm salt water to soothe throat irritation
Avoid smoke, dust, and strong fumes; keep the living area well-ventilated
Cover your mouth and nose with a cloth, tissue, or your elbow when coughing, and wash hands often
Avoid smoking and, where possible, second-hand smoke
Use a simple home remedy such as warm water with honey (avoid honey for infants under one year of age) if culturally practised and safe for the person
Wear a mask around others if you have an ongoing cough, to protect family members while the cause is being checked
If the cough does not improve within one to two weeks despite rest and home care, it is time to have it checked at a health facility.
When to Seek Medical Attention
Please visit the nearest health sub-centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), or hospital promptly if you notice any of the following:
Cough lasting two weeks or more
Blood in the cough or sputum
Difficulty breathing, fast breathing, or shortness of breath
Chest pain or tightness
High or persistent fever, especially with night sweats
Unexplained weight loss or ongoing loss of appetite
Cough in an infant, young child, elderly person, pregnant woman, or someone with an existing illness (such as diabetes, HIV, or malnutrition)
Bluish lips or face, or severe weakness/confusion (seek emergency care immediately)
A cough lasting two weeks or longer is a key warning sign for tuberculosis (TB) in India. TB testing and treatment are provided free of cost at government health facilities under the national TB elimination programme. Getting checked early protects both your health and the health of your family.
Odisha-Specific Notes
The Odisha Department of Health & Family Welfare, through the State TB Cell and the National Health Mission, conducts regular community TB screening camps (Shivirs) across all districts, including rural and hard-to-reach areas, to find and treat people with prolonged cough early.
Free cough and TB screening is available at Health & Wellness Centres, PHCs, CHCs, and district hospitals across Odisha
Ni-kshay Mitras (community volunteers) and ASHA/ANM workers can help connect people with a persistent cough to the nearest testing centre
During monsoon and winter months, indoor smoke from cooking fires and damp housing conditions common in parts of rural Odisha can worsen coughs; improving ventilation at home can help
If you or a family member has had a cough for two weeks or more, ask your local ASHA worker or nearest health facility about free TB testing
Source Basis
This content is based on general public health guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO), the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the National Health Mission (NHM), the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (Central TB Division), and the Odisha Department of Health & Family Welfare. It reflects commonly published, general awareness-level information and is written in simple language for a broad audience; it does not reproduce any source text directly.
